thesis: American Water Works is the largest investor-owned water and wastewater utility in the United States. **[Fact]** The company serves about **3.6 million** active customers across **14 states** through regulated local monopoly franchises (`investor-documents/sec-edgar/10-K_20260218_rpt20251231_acc0001410636_26_000034.htm`). **[Fact]** FY2025 consolidated operating revenue was **$5.14 billion** (up **9.7%** versus **$4.68 billion** in FY2024). **[Fact]** The **Regulated Businesses** segment contributed **$4.72 billion** (**92%** of revenue); **Market-Based Businesses** contributed **$417 million** (**8%**). **[Fact]** FY2025 diluted earnings per share were **$5.69** on net income of **$1.11 billion**; operating cash flow was **$2.06 billion** while capital spending was **$3.13 billion**. **[Inference]** Owner economics are set by state public utility commissions through allowed returns on rate-base investment, not open-market water pricing.
why_market_wrong: There is **no classic dated mispricing signal** (HK predictive attribute: **none**). **[Inference]** Generalists may treat AWK as a bond-proxy utility and anchor on dividend yield (~2.2% at ~$130) while underweighting rate-base growth funded by heavy capital spending that eventually flows into earnings. **[Fact]** In October 2025 the company announced a **stock-for-stock merger with Essential Utilities**; shareholders approved the deal on **February 10, 2026**, with expected close by **Q1 2027** pending regulatory approvals (`DEF 14A_20260324...htm`). **[Inference]** The market may be pricing merger completion risk and integration uncertainty rather than standalone regulated earnings power. **[Inference]** Bears may focus on negative GAAP free cash flow (capex exceeds operating cash flow) without crediting regulatory recovery of growth investment through infrastructure surcharges and general rate cases.
